subject: biology
hotspotPositionNote: position [x,y,z] values below are provisional estimates derived from the asset brief's stated proportions (2.2-unit-long, 0.7-unit-diameter capsule body centered at the origin, long axis on world X, flagellated pole at +X). They must be recalculated against the actual GLB geometry once the model is produced, before these coordinates are relied on for hotspot placement in the viewer.

hotspots.label: Cell Membrane
hotspots.positionHint: Thin boundary layer just inside the cell wall, placed at the mid-length equator of the rod where the cross-section cut is most visible
hotspots.description: A thin, flexible layer just inside the cell wall that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
hotspots.definition: A thin, flexible layer of fats and proteins that forms the inner boundary of the cell.
hotspots.function: Controls which nutrients, water, and waste molecules move into and out of the cell.
hotspots.location: Sits directly beneath the rigid cell wall, wrapping the entire cell and lining the cytoplasm.
hotspots.whyItMatters: It's the checkpoint for everything entering or leaving the cell, so many disinfectants and some antibiotics work by damaging this layer until the cell can no longer control its own contents.

relatedConcept.label: Cell Wall
relatedConcept.reason: The membrane and the wall sit right next to each other but do different jobs — membrane controls traffic in and out, wall provides rigid shape and protection — and learners commonly conflate the two.

hotspots.label: Cytoplasm
hotspots.positionHint: Interior gel-fill volume, visible once the cross-section cut plane is active; hotspot floats near the center of the exposed interior
hotspots.description: The jelly-like fluid filling the inside of the cell where chemical reactions and floating structures live.
hotspots.definition: The gel-like fluid that fills the interior of the cell.
hotspots.function: Provides the watery medium where chemical reactions happen and where the DNA and ribosomes float freely.
hotspots.location: Fills the entire interior of the cell, bounded on all sides by the cell membrane.
hotspots.whyItMatters: Because bacteria have no internal compartments, everything that happens inside the cell — building proteins, breaking down nutrients, copying DNA — happens together in this one shared space, so a single chemical change in the cytoplasm can affect the whole cell at once.

relatedConcept.label: Nucleus
relatedConcept.reason: A eukaryotic cell's cytoplasm is organized around a membrane-bound nucleus and other organelles; a bacterium's cytoplasm is one open space with nothing walled off, which is the core prokaryote-vs-eukaryote contrast.

hotspots.label: DNA (Nucleoid)
hotspots.positionHint: Irregular tangled blob positioned slightly off-center within the cytoplasm, roughly one-third along the rod's length from the non-flagellated pole
hotspots.description: A loosely coiled tangle of DNA sitting free in the cytoplasm, since bacteria have no nucleus to hold it in.
hotspots.definition: The cell's single circular chromosome, loosely coiled together in a region called the nucleoid.
hotspots.function: Stores the genetic instructions the cell uses to build proteins and to copy itself during reproduction.
hotspots.location: Floats freely within the cytoplasm, off-center, not enclosed by any membrane of its own.
hotspots.whyItMatters: Because the nucleoid has no membrane around it, the cell's entire genetic library is directly exposed to the cytoplasm — this is the single biggest structural difference between a bacterium and one of your own cells, and it's exactly what a nucleus-less cell means in practice.

relatedConcept.label: Nucleus
relatedConcept.reason: The nucleoid does the same basic job as a eukaryotic nucleus — housing the cell's DNA — but without a surrounding membrane, making this the clearest direct comparison point between the two cell types.

hotspots.label: Ribosome
hotspots.positionHint: One representative dot from the scattered cluster of small ribosome instances distributed through the cytoplasm, picked near the upper-right of the exposed cross-section
hotspots.description: One of thousands of tiny particles scattered through the cytoplasm that build proteins from genetic instructions.
hotspots.definition: A tiny molecular machine, smaller than the ribosomes in human cells, that reads genetic instructions and links amino acids into proteins.
hotspots.function: Builds every protein the cell needs to grow, repair itself, and function.
hotspots.location: Scattered in large numbers throughout the cytoplasm.
hotspots.whyItMatters: Bacterial (70S) ribosomes are a different size and shape from human (80S) ribosomes, so many antibiotics are designed to jam bacterial ribosomes specifically — stopping the bacteria's protein production without harming the patient's own cells.

relatedConcept.label: 80S Ribosome (Eukaryotic)
relatedConcept.reason: Comparing the bacterial 70S ribosome to the larger eukaryotic 80S ribosome explains why some antibiotics can target bacteria selectively without harming human cells.

hotspots.label: Cell Wall
hotspots.positionHint: Outer rigid shell of the rod, hotspot placed on the exterior surface at the widest point of the capsule shape, opposite the flagellum
hotspots.description: A rigid outer layer outside the membrane that gives the bacterium its shape and protects it from bursting.
hotspots.definition: A rigid outer layer built mainly from a mesh-like molecule called peptidoglycan.
hotspots.function: Gives the cell its fixed rod shape and keeps it from swelling up and bursting.
hotspots.location: The outermost layer of the cell, surrounding the cell membrane.
hotspots.whyItMatters: Peptidoglycan doesn't exist in human cells, so several major antibiotic families (like penicillin) work by blocking its construction — weakening the wall until the bacterium bursts, while leaving the patient's own wall-free cells untouched.

relatedConcept.label: Peptidoglycan
relatedConcept.reason: The cell wall's protective strength comes specifically from peptidoglycan, the molecule that most cell-wall-targeting antibiotics are built to disrupt.

hotspots.label: Flagellum
hotspots.positionHint: Thin tapering whip-like tail extending outward from one pole of the rod; hotspot placed at the midpoint of its length
hotspots.description: A long, whip-like tail that rotates like a propeller to move the bacterium through liquid.
hotspots.definition: A long, whip-like tail built from coiled protein filaments.
hotspots.function: Rotates like a propeller, driven by a tiny motor at its base, to push the cell through liquid.
hotspots.location: Extends outward from one pole (end) of the rod-shaped cell.
hotspots.whyItMatters: The flagellum lets a bacterium steer itself toward food or away from harmful chemicals (a behavior called chemotaxis), which directly affects how infections spread and how bacteria colonize new environments.

relatedConcept.label: Cilia
relatedConcept.reason: Cilia are the short, hair-like movement structures found on some eukaryotic cells — comparing them to a bacterium's single long flagellum highlights how differently prokaryotes and eukaryotes solve the same problem of movement.

visualStyleNotes: Match Anatomy Atelier exactly: model renders as a single hero object centered on a warm off-white (near #F7F3EC) background/ground with no environment clutter, soft even studio lighting (large soft key + gentle fill, no hard specular hotspots, no rim-light glow), minimal chrome around the viewer frame. Material is matte-satin, not glossy/plastic and not metallic — think soft biological tissue with a faint warm subsurface-scattering fake (slightly lit-from-within look via a soft Fresnel-driven color lift, not a bloom/glow effect). Apply Quantaora's biology accent palette restrained and desaturated: warm coral for the cell wall/membrane, muted leaf green for the cytoplasm fill, warm paper/cream as the base undertone, graphite-navy for the nucleoid tangle for contrast. Absolutely no neon/saturated "germ cartoon" colors, no cartoon eyes/face, no bump-mapped pimply skin texture, no baked-in text labels, no glossy plastic toy look, and no gradient/glow halos anywhere — flat, calm, scientific-illustration lighting only. Hotspot dots are small solid-color circles (colored per layer, consistent with the app's existing hotspot dot language) that sit flush on or just above the surface and open a structure card on click; they must read as elegant and precise, not gamey pins or bouncing markers.
assetBrief:
DELIVERABLE: one GLB (glTF 2.0 binary, Draco-compressed geometry, embedded textures under 4K) named bacterial-cell.glb, plus a thumbnail PNG render matching the default camera framing below.

SHAPE & PROPORTIONS: Model a rod-shaped bacillus bacterium (E. coli-like), not a coccus (sphere) or spirillum (spiral) — rod shape is the clearest teaching silhouette for this component. Body is a stadium/capsule form: a cylinder with hemispherical (gently rounded, not pointed) end caps. Length-to-diameter ratio approximately 3:1 (e.g. 2.2 units long, 0.7 units diameter). Model origin sits at the geometric center of the rod, long axis aligned to world X, so auto-rotate spins around a natural axis. Surface should have very subtle organic undulation (not a hard mechanical cylinder) but stay clean and simple — this is a diagrammatic anatomical asset, not a hyper-realistic microbe render.

LAYERED CONSTRUCTION (build as separate, independently toggle-able mesh nodes, named to match conceptIds for hotspot/layer binding):
1. `flagellum` — a single long, thin, gently tapering tube (helical/wavy, 2–3 soft undulations, not a straight spike) attached at one pole, extending outward roughly 1.5x the body length. Slightly translucent, lighter tone than the wall.
2. `cellWall` — the rigid outer shell of the rod, solid coral-toned matte material. This is the outermost visible surface in the default (non-cross-section) view.
3. `cellMembrane` — a very thin shell just inside the wall, only exposed when the wall is toggled off or the cross-section is active. Slightly different warm tone from the wall so the two layers read as distinct in cross-section.
4. `cytoplasm` — the interior fill volume, muted leaf-green translucent-matte material, only visible via cross-section or layer isolation.
5. `nucleoid` — one irregular, loosely tangled blob (think a soft scribble/knot shape, asymmetric, NOT a smooth sphere) positioned off-center within the cytoplasm, graphite-navy tone for contrast. This should visually read as "loose coiled thread," distinguishing it from a nucleus (which this cell deliberately lacks).
6. `ribosomes` — 40–80 small instanced spheres (uniform tiny size, roughly 1/40th of body diameter) scattered evenly through the cytoplasm volume, slightly darker/warmer than the cytoplasm so they read as discrete particles, not noise.

CROSS-SECTION: Build the model so a single planar cut along the long axis (through the center, perpendicular to Y or Z) cleanly exposes all interior layers in the correct order (wall → membrane → cytoplasm with visible nucleoid + ribosomes) with clean capped cut-faces (no z-fighting, no open non-manifold geometry at the cut plane). This powers the viewer's cross-section toggle described in spec §13.

MATERIALS: Matte-satin PBR (roughness ~0.55–0.7, near-zero metalness) for all layers. No glossy highlights, no metallic sheen, no emissive glow. Use flat/gradient procedural coloring rather than printed texture maps — no baked text, no seams, no photographic bacterial texture. Palette: cell wall coral (~#E8846B family), membrane a slightly lighter warm coral-cream, cytoplasm muted leaf green (~#8FAE7D family) at moderate opacity so the nucleoid/ribosomes are visible through it in cross-section, nucleoid graphite-navy (~#3A3F4B family), ribosomes a warm mid-tone that contrasts against the green cytoplasm, flagellum pale warm cream, slightly translucent.

SCALE & EXPORT: Stylized display scale (not real micrometer scale) — treat the whole rod as roughly 2–2.5 world units long so it fills the default camera frame with headroom. Poly budget: keep total under ~25k triangles (body + flagellum + ribosome instances combined) for smooth mobile performance; use instancing for the ribosome cluster rather than 80 unique meshes. UV-unwrap primary shells even though textures are flat-colored, in case future detail passes need them. Deliver with Y-up orientation, centered origin, and clean named node hierarchy (`cellWall`, `cellMembrane`, `cytoplasm`, `nucleoid`, `ribosomes`, `flagellum`) so the app's layer-toggle and hotspot systems can bind directly to node names without remapping.

DEFAULT CAMERA: position [2.6, 1.3, 3.0], target [0, 0, 0] — a calm 3/4 elevated view showing the rod's length, the flagellum trailing off one end, and enough of the body surface to place all wall/membrane hotspots legibly; auto-rotate is on by default per the component's autoRotateDefault.

DO NOT: give it cartoon eyes, a face, or personality; use bright saturated "germ mascot" colors (hot pink, neon green, etc.); add bumpy pimple/pore texture or a wet/slimy glossy shader; add background props, petri dish, or environment — it must render as an isolated hero object on transparent/off-white per Anatomy Atelier framing; bake any text/labels into textures; make the nucleoid a smooth sphere (it must read as an irregular free-floating tangle, the entire teaching point being "no nucleus"); make the flagellum a rigid straight spike (it should read as a flexible whip/propeller).
